bearings.paper_claim: In the weight-proportional competitive LT model (Eq. 1) the A-spread is not monotone (Theorem 1: root A-probability 11/40 before and 103/400 after adding one A seed, Appendix A Theorem 12) and not submodular (Theorem 2). The Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher greedy bound does not transfer to that model.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2, Eq. 1, Theorems 1-2; Appendix A Theorems 12-13, Figure 1
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b) (flip_model.py 92-97) has the form of Eq. 1, but a and b each add a money term to WP*nA/mAt, so it is not the same model. Stance is fixed inside a run, so the objective is separable by member. optimize.py checks concavity at run time (concavity_violations) and labels only the fixed-state run as fixed_state_lazy_greedy. A modeled conversion re-runs topic_setup, where mAt = max(nA) (flip_model.py 138-140), so one conversion can lower another member's WP*nA/mAt term. Such a run is labeled modeled_threshold_replanning (optimize.py 190) and carries no certificate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Structural analogy only. Borodin non-monotonicity runs through multi-step propagation under random thresholds, which pflip does not have. The conversion-path concern applies only when conversion_reachable is true. Whether the mAt renormalisation lowers total winnability after a conversion is not measured in this text.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers and theorem locations confirmed in the text. Code lines confirmed. The analyst called the fixed-state objective concave; the code only tests concavity at run time and the docstring asserts diminishing returns, so the wording is now checked, not proven. The Eq. 1 match is partial because the money term is absent from Borodin model.

bearings.paper_claim: With technology-specific edge weights, the separated-threshold competitive problem (Theorem 7) and the Carnes wave-propagation variant with technology-specific probabilities (Theorem 8) are NP-hard to approximate within Omega(N^(1/2-eps)) by a Vertex Cover reduction (Appendix D, Theorem 16). This refutes the Carnes et al. conjecture for that case.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5, Theorems 7-8; Appendix D, Theorem 16, Figure 3
bearings.system_side: The engine builds one kernel P = build_P(adj) and uses it for both colours (budget_frontier.py 77, per_topic_coalition.py 37, scenario.py 39). Pro and anti frontiers draw the same keyed splitmix value per (iteration, edge) (budget_frontier.py 83-94; per_topic_coalition.py 44-55), and the first colour to reach a node keeps it. The paper states its hardness for models with separate per-technology edge weights, so the shared kernel sits outside that stated scope. The paper does not describe the Bharathi-Kempe-Salek weights, so calling them shared-weight is the analyst reading, not the paper.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only while the kernel stays shared. Giving anti-side diffusion its own edge weights or physics, such as cpf_pressure on the B side only (moneyball_core.py 546), would move the engine into the stated hardness scope. Tie-breaking by frontier order is not analysed in this paper.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper theorem locations and the shared-kernel code are confirmed. The label shared-weight Bharathi-Kempe-Salek family is not in Borodin text, which says only that greedy has been applied to competitive extensions [2,1]. Scope statement kept, label removed.

bearings.paper_claim: Most natural competitive extensions lose submodularity. Monotonicity can survive while submodularity fails (Theorems 3-6). The greedy (1-1/e) guarantee is shown only for the OR model with monotone submodular decision functions (Theorems 9-11). Section 7 leaves other models open.
bearings.system_side: budget_frontier.py runs a CELF-style lazy greedy on a heap. spread() applies the seed gate (line 128) and removes activated contest seeds from the anti set (line 131). marg() multiplies the raw gain by fac, which is REPFAC times leverage for contest seeds (line 143, applied at 156), and floors at zero. audit_frontier.py 27-35 counts marginal inversions on clamped spread and passes up to 35 percent of marginals as MC noise (tolerance 0.35 times the marginal count).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies to electoral mode (contest and defend seeds). This paper gives no submodularity result for the electoral objective. Any coalition-mode greedy guarantee comes from the competitive IC literature cited to Bharathi et al. (Borodin ref 1), not from this paper, so coalition-only mode is not covered here. Separating MC noise from structure needs a read-only check of raw marginals under common random numbers.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper theorem locations and claims confirmed. Code lines confirmed, including the marginal and fac logic at budget_frontier.py 153-156 and the 35 percent tolerance. The claims that Bharathi proof excludes contest seeds and that coalition-only mode is closer to a provable case are not in Borodin text, so they are removed as paper-based support.

bearings.paper_claim: In the separated-threshold competitive LT model a node is activated by whichever technology weighted active neighbours first exceed that technology own threshold. Adding A seeds never raises the probability that B propagates (Lemma 3 part 1, used in Theorem 3), but the process is not submodular in general (Theorem 4, counterexample only in an unincluded full version).
bearings.system_side: lt_priming.py prime() (96-103) sets theta from the tier ladder (base THETA runs from 0.0 for Ally to 3.0 for Opponent, lines 19-21), adds a committed-opponent term and a money-captured term, and sums pressure over pro sources only (proset). Anti neighbours exert no competing threshold pressure. The recruit search (131-140) picks cheapest recruits per target rather than optimising a seed set, so submodularity is not invoked.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Thresholds here are not normalised to Borodin uniform [0,1] draws (base ladder 0.0 to 3.0 plus additive terms). Adding an anti-side threshold would be a model change for Paul to decide. Borodin monotonicity result is for the separated-threshold model and says nothing about this solver recruit lists, for which the paper gives no guarantee.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claims and code lines confirmed. The threshold range should read 0.0 (Ally) to 3.0 (Opponent) in the base ladder, not 0.6 to 3.0. The claim that Borodin separated-threshold model is the natural competitive version of this solver is the analyst suggestion, not stated in the paper. Lemma 3 part 1 is the B-monotonicity source; Theorem 3 is about A.

related.why: Borodin cites Bharathi-Kempe-Salek [1] among works that applied the greedy approach to competitive extensions. The system competitive cascade follows that family, and Borodin results mark where the guarantee stops for LT variants. Borodin does not say Bharathi follower problem keeps the guarantee.

Borodin does not cite Golovin-Krause. The link is through the code: optimize.py uses a Golovin-Krause data-dependent upper bound as a diagnostic. Borodin shows which competitive objectives lose the submodularity such bounds need.

Competitive influence maximization in voter dynamics with timing and network heterogeneity. Its text does not cite Borodin or discuss submodularity, so it is a neighbouring competitive-IM study on a different diffusion model, not a follow-up to Borodin.
Heuristics for competitive continuous influence maximisation under voting dynamics. A practical alternative when Borodin-style results remove greedy guarantees.
Learned policies for complex-contagion seeding, which the text describes as non-submodular. Fits Borodin finding that threshold competition breaks submodularity.
Compares greedy CELF++ with sampling and centrality heuristics on cost-effectiveness. Relevant once Borodin shows greedy has no guarantee in most competitive LT variants.

summary_issues: summary_md says the FLIP objective is separable and concave so the exact certificate holds. The code only checks concavity at run time (concavity_violations in optimize.py) and conditions the certificate on that check. Reword as checked, not proven.

summary_md and flags say FLIP is not any of Borodin four models. It is closest to the Section 2 weight-proportional split but has no thresholds or propagation, so the accurate claim is that it is not that model either.
